items.body:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

…

items.body:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

items.body:
## pliavo’s folding piano compresses seven octaves

Denver-based Pliavo introduces its Fold-and-Go Piano, a portable digital [instrument](https://www.designboom.com/tag/musical-instruments/) whose 84 keys collapse into a compact bundle small enough to carry inside a backpack. Each octave occupies its own rigid section, and a system of hinges allows the otherwise standard [black-and-white](https://www.designboom.com/tag/black-and-white/) keyboard to fold accordion-style into a vertical stack.

At its full length, the seven-octave instrument stretches 113 centimeters (44.5 inches) across a tabletop. Once folded, it measures just 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) along its length and weighs under two pounds. The team has also developed a smaller, five-octave edition with 60 keys.

Pliavo develops a collapsible 84-key digital piano | images courtesy Pliavo via Kickstarter

## a hinged alternative to the roll-up keyboard

Part of the appeal of Pliavo’s [design](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/pliavo/pliavo-the-84-key-piano-that-goes-with-you) is that it retains the physical geometry of a conventional keyboard. While many compact electronic pianos take the form of flexible silicone mats, here the musician plays across a continuous arrangement of rigid keys with three millimeters of vertical travel.

The mechanics of the folding design come with some compromises. The keys are unweighted and lack velocity sensitivity, which limits the expressive range of the instrument. Pliavo equips the piano with a detachable wireless speaker and a rechargeable battery designed to last around five hours.

a detachable wireless speaker accompanies the portable keyboard

## a portable instrument for music on the move

The piano’s internal sound library comprises 128 instrument tones alongside an equally extensive selection of rhythm patterns. Through Bluetooth or a USB-C connection, the keyboard doubles as a MIDI controller. For a musician traveling with a laptop, an entire seven-octave workspace could occupy a small corner of their luggage.

Pliavo [launched](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/pliavo/pliavo-the-84-key-piano-that-goes-with-you) the instrument on Kickstarter in November 2026 and has already exceeded its initial funding goal. The team has developed a playable prototype, with refinements to its sound and finishes underway ahead of an anticipated February 2027 delivery.

items.body:
When Siddhartha Gautama gave his first teaching after enlightenment, it was to five friends in the deer park at Sarnath, not far from Varanasi in the Ganges Valley. Wanting to transmit to them the essence of his breakthrough, he crystallized his insights into what would become known as the four noble truths. These include the truth of the way out of suffering, known as the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

The eightfold path offers a way to touch awakening as Gautama did. These insights were not the result of thinking or study, nor were they a creed or philosophical doctrine. They were the fruit of Gautama’s own direct experience and meditative realization, and they conveyed a path that traced a “middle way” between the two extremes of asceticism and indulgence. It was a way, he believed, that could lead anyone to realize understanding, liberation, and peace.

#### “You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes.”

As a species we’re still struggling to find a middle way, to steer a wise course through the extremes of fanaticism, greed, nihilism, rage, and despair. The ancient wisdom of the eightfold path offers eight matrixes that are powerfully relevant today as a guide to help us navigate these extremes and bring a meaningful direction to our daily lives, actions, and relationships.

All elements of the eightfold path inter-are. You cannot extract any of them from the context of the path. So, for example, if you take mindfulness out of the ethical context of the path, it is no longer right mindfulness. All eight elements are interrelated and interdependent. They enhance each other. When practiced deeply, each element of the path contains the other seven within it, and they complement each other to create a complete path to liberation.

My teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught that right mindfulness is at the heart of the eightfold path. So, with the energy of right mindfulness as the foundation, we’re able to develop right concentration. This gives rise to insight or “right view,” which Thich Nhat Hanh described as the “insight of interbeing.” It is this deep view of the world that guides us to an ethical and beneficial life through right thinking, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort. So, when you generate the energy of mindfulness, you are naturally concentrated on the object of your mindfulness, whether it’s your breathing, your body, the sunset, or the presence of the person in front of you.

Photo © Noumae | Dreamstime.com

The energies of mindfulness and concentration naturally give rise to insight, right view. You touch the insight of interbeing between your breath and the earth, or between your body and your ancestors and descendants, or between your heart and the sun in the sky. You realize that you inter-are with the person in front of you.
Already, this insight of interbeing helps us touch peace, joy, and freedom.

Now, with the energy of mindfulness, concentration, and insight, your thinking will naturally be right thinking.

It will be free from discrimination and separation, and on the basis of that thinking, your speech will be right speech and your action right action.

Cultivating right diligence (or effort) in that moment, you’ll be able to see and calm any unwholesome seeds that may get triggered in your consciousness, such as anger or despair, and identify and activate positive seeds, such as gratitude and compassion. With all those energies alive in you, the way you spend your time, energy, and labor—your livelihood—will be “right.” It will be beneficial for you and everyone around you.

# A Jazz Walk Incoming — Roden Newsletter Archive

### RodenIssue #120November 22, 2026

## A Jazz Walk Incoming

### Twenty-one days of chasing jazz and Shōwa in Kyūshū

Roden Readers —

Fall! Finally! Jacket weather! Sweaters! Snow on Fuji! Oh, my!

What has been going on this past month? A whole lotta hermiting. I’ve been on a decidedly teenager-like (or Mishima-like, if you prefer; the man almost never rose before noon) schedule, which my body clock seems to love, working late into the night and passing out around two or three and then waking up around ten or eleven, pounding a big ol’ smoothie, and then working like mad from noon to six, breaking for a nice dinner with friends, and then diving back under until my futon calls. This is an ideal schedule for me. Because I am insane. I basically never shifted back from Europe time to Japan time in October. Also, a smoothie + slow, delicious dinner turns out to be a great eating schedule? I feel light and energetic. Am I an adult? I’m not sure. I do push-ups and walk 10,000 steps a day. Such is the glamorous life of being self-employed at forty-six years old while the world speedruns its own unique flavor of insanity in the background. Is the singularity here yet?

#### #SHŌWA! COLOSSUS!

My big announcement here is a new pop-up newsletter / “tour” starting in two days (on Wednesday the 25th). It’s called: SHŌWA㍼COLOSSUS.

Sign up here (as with all my pop-ups, you have to enthusiastically opt in):.

For twenty-one+ days I’ll be on the road visiting some of the last remaining classic jazz kissas of Kyūshū. As usual, I’ll be sending daily dispatches and more. As usual, I have no idea what we’ll discover. And as usual, I am forever grateful to my SPECIAL PROJECTS members who make projects like this possible. All funding and support for these tours (which are complicated, expensive, slightly crazy affairs) comes directly from memberships and book sales.

If you don’t mind sharing the Ridgeline link, or the Instagram post, please do. These tours are one of the few chances to grow my audience without having to be a full-time social media bobblehead. I appreciate it!

#### #Holiday Presents?

Thank you to everyone who has grabbed a notebook! They’re almost sold out. We have about fifty sets left. If I make some more, it won’t be until next year.

Things Become Other Things, the hardcover black-and-white Random House edition, is available for a paltry $18 shipped from the Evil™ Amazon® (and probably about $25 book-in-hand from your local bookshop, which you should go to, say hello to the people working there, smile at a few customers, smell the smells of literal tons of paper lined up on the walls; and if they don’t have a copy and you request one, a thousand baby kittens are instantly born into loving families).

Here’s what’s available in the fancy SPECIAL PROJECTS shop:

- Kissa by Kissa 6th ed., unsigned
- Things Become Other Things, fine art 2nd ed., signed
- OTHER THING, first ed., signed
- ⬤ — a made-in-Japan lay-flat notebook (I should have signed these)
Just a reminder, SPECIAL PROJECTS members get big discounts on everything in the SP Shop. And shipping for an order with multiple items is a significantly better deal than single items (just the way DHL works; the first kilogram is the most expensive). Orders ship next business day from my warehouse in Osaka, and arrive almost everywhere around the world in (usually) 2-3 days. It’s very efficient! These all make good presents.

We just — finally! — sold the last Tomato Farmer’s print. Thank you to everyone who bought one over the years. One of my goals for next year is to do more printing (working with local high-end photo shops doing C-prints?). Maybe even do a show at some point? I have a huge back catalogue of shots (many now with negatives) and should probably do something with some of them.

items.body:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled *Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories*. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

## Fostering connections and reflection

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. [Uri Hasson](https://blog.ted.com/what-happens-in-the-brain-when-we-hear-stories-uri-hasson-at-ted2016/) and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at [UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft/oral-history-center) for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

> I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

## Providing unique perspectives

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the [Oral History Association](https://oralhistory.org/), “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of [Voice of Witness](https://voiceofwitness.org/), a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

items.body:
# The human voice

This is a post from Robin Sloan’s lab blog & notebook. You can visit the blog’s homepage, or learn more about me.

## The human voice

November 20, 2026

I encourage you to open Levent Alpöge’s PDF note announcing his proof of the Rie­mann Hypoth­esis with the help of AI — because although the work was AI-assisted, this note is so clearly and beau­ti­fully human. It’s fabulous.

I have noticed the steady creep of AI-generated text into the pub­li­ca­tions of the big AI com­pa­nies themselves, and while it tends not to be on the level of “egregious slop”, it does lend every­thing a … smoothness. I note also that these pub­li­ca­tions are very rarely signed; they come from The Blob. Who wrote this?Who wrote this? I know it’s cus­tomary for big com­pa­nies to speak Blob-like, but/and I still find it jarring.

Coun­ter­point Alpöge: his note is not only better than a smooth, AI-generated summation, it’s also better than an aca­d­emic paper, because his passion — his appre­ci­a­tion of sur­prise and beauty — is so clear on the page. It seems almost to rise off the screen, a 3D layer of sparkling energy.

Tell you what, you can use all the AI you want in your project, if you write about it like this, in your real human voice.

P.S. And then there’s this, the absolute sig­na­ture of our new era: “The Rie­mann Hypoth­esis is proven, but not yet understood.”

# A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style - James Stone

## A free multi-CDN, jsDelivr style

28 Nov 26 post 1674 words #webdev #cdn #dns jsDelivr does something I have always found neat: it does not use one CDN, it uses several, and for every user it picks whichever one is fastest for them.fastest for them right now.right now, based on RUM. I wanted to see how close I could get to that on free tiers only. Plus the vanity of it is kinda nice. How many people can say their site is served from ~660340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly340+ Cloudflare, 210+ Gcore and 114 Fastly, as at Nov 2026 data centers globally.

The experiment lives at cdn.jamesst.one, which now serves a copy of this site, and you can watch where it is routing at rum.jamesst.one.

### How a normal CDN works

A plain server has one IP address in one place, so every visitor’s packets travel all the way to it. A CDN instead announces the same IP address from hundreds of locations,from hundreds of locations at once (this is called anycast: one address, many machines, and the network decides which one you reach), and internet routing (BGP) delivers each visitor to the nearest one. That location serves a cached copy, and only goes back to the origin on a cache miss. For example, 151.101.1.242, one of Fastly’s addresses this site uses, answers in 0.6 to 2 ms from Globalping probes in Copenhagen, Singapore and Melbourne alike. No single machine can be that close to all three.

The above diagram is actually a simplification, because before that, a client first has to look up the IP address to connect to, i.e. DNS. A multi-CDN hooks into the DNS reply and picks which CDN is best, then that CDN’s anycast picks which specific data center based on network routing rules.

### How it fits together

The CDN is chosen in DNS. When your resolver asks for cdn.jamesst.one, the answer is a CNAME to one of three CDNs, and which one depends on where you are. Or, more accurately, the network you are on.

- DNS:Gcore Managed DNS. Its free plan supports “dynamic” records: a set of answers with metadata (countries, continents, networks) and pickers that choose one per query.
- The CDNs: Fastly, Gcore CDN and Cloudflare Pages. All three pull from the same origin and add the same response headers, plus a Server-Timing: cdn;desc="fastly" style header so every measurement knows who served it.
- rumd:rumd, the RUM daemon, as in Real User Monitoring: a small Go service that collects measurements, scores each CDN per country, continent and network, and recommends a routing policy.
- dnsctl: applies that recommendation to Gcore, but only once it has been stable for a few checks and a minimum interval has passed, so DNS does not flap.
### The free tier gotchas

ThingWhat I hitCloudflareThe free plan only proxies a domain if Cloudflare hosts its DNS. Cloudflare for SaaS (custom hostnames) works with outside DNS, but needs a root domain zone in your account, and I wanted DNS to stay on Gcore. Cloudflare Pages saved the day: a Pages project accepts a subdomain on someone else’s DNS as a custom domain. A tiny Worker in the project proxies to the origin and adds the headers.Gcore DNSOne dynamic record set, at most three records, minimum TTL 120s. So at most three CDNs can be live at once. (I checked: a fourth record is refused.)CertificatesEvery CDN has to prove it controls cdn.jamesst.one. Fastly uses a DNS challenge, but Gcore and Cloudflare Pages validate over HTTP, which only works while DNS sends the validator to them. The first certificate meant pointing DNS at Pages for a few seconds. Renewals are a problem I have not fully solved.

### Measuring without JavaScript

The first version used a small script on the page that read Resource Timing entries and beaconed them home. Which works but I would rather not put JS on pages for this. jsDelivr itself gets its RUM data from elsewhere: I think it used Cedexis, then PerfOps, rather than running a script of its own.

…

# Let's Play with Hardcaml! - Metasepi

## Let's Play with Hardcaml!

Posted on November 28, 2026 / Tags: takibi, fpga, ocaml, hardcaml

### Table of contents

I prepared a five-minute lightning talk for the 8th Homebrew CPU Meetup on November 28, 2026. The slides are below.

Open slides in a new tab · Download PDF · View Markdown source

This talk is a gentle introduction to Hardcaml, an RTL design library embedded in OCaml. Rather than discussing advanced verification techniques, I wanted to share the fun of building digital circuits in an interactive programming environment.

We start with a simple 5-bit counter and do everything inside utop, an OCaml REPL:

- Describe a digital circuit using ordinary OCaml functions.
- Generate Verilog from the circuit.
- Simulate the circuit cycle by cycle using an ordinary OCaml for loop.
- Display the recorded waveforms directly in the terminal.
No FPGA, external Verilog simulator, or even a separate OCaml project is needed to try this example. I tested the installation steps and the REPL session in a Docker environment, so you can follow along with the slides.

And what happens if we keep playing with Hardcaml?

With the help of AI coding agents, I ended up building a dual-core RISC-V SoC that boots Linux 6.18 with SMP on a Colorlight i9 FPGA board.

I hope this talk encourages more people to give Hardcaml a try and enjoy building their own digital circuits.

## The Contents of Perception

In contemporary philosophy, the phrase ’the contents of perception’ means, roughly, what is conveyed to the subject by her perceptual experience. For example, suppose you are looking into a piano at the array of hammers and strings. There will be a way these things look to you when you see them: they will look to have a certain shape, color, texture, and arrangement relative to one another, among other things. Your visual experience conveys to you that the piano has these features. If your experience is illusory in some respect then the piano won’t really have all those features. But even then, there will still be something conveyed to you by your experience. Three main questions will be addressed in this entry. First (Sections 1–2), what are contents and what is their relation to experiences? Second (Sections 3–7), which contents are contents of experience? Finally (Section 8), in virtue of what do experiences have contents, when they do?

## 1. What are Perceptual Experiences?

This entry will focus exclusively on the contents of perceptual experiences . It is definitional of experience, as the term is used here, that they have some phenomenal character, or more briefly, some phenomenology. The phenomenology of an experience is what it is like for the subject to have it. At any given waking moment, one normally has experiences in some (perhaps all) of the five sense modalities, along with proprioceptive experience of some sort. Like occurrent emotions and background moods, these contribute to one’s overall experience . Each of five sense modalities seems to be accompanied by a distinctive kind of phenomenology. Sometimes the boundaries between them can be hard to draw, for example between olfactory and gustatory phenomenology, kinesthetic experience and haptic-tactile experience (that is, tactile experiences involving movement rather than just pressure sensation), and perhaps, in some cases, between the latter two and visual experience (on the last point see Press et al . 2004, Kennett et al . 2001, Fotopoulou et al . 2009; on distinguishing the senses, see Stokes, Matthen and Briggs 2014, Wilson and Macpherson 2018). In general, it is an open question how holistic perceptual experiences, and to what extent it can be viewed as an aggregate of separable experiences in distinct modalities. Despite these difficulties, some rough distinctions can be drawn: the difference between seeing red and seeing blue is not a difference in how things sound, or in how one’s body feels.

Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that "explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete".

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as "a refuge between the mountains and the sea".

"One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape," said Estúdio 41, an architectural firm based in Curitiba.

Drawings and photographs

Previous

Next

Drawings and photographs

Close

Ground floor plan

First floor plan

Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.

The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.

"At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house's skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape," the team said.

To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).

It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

The system consists of six columns, four beams and 20 double-tee slabs, also known as "π" (pi)-shaped slabs. The latter are pre-stressed concrete panels with a cross-section that resembles the Greek letter π.

"The project explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete," said the team.

Read:

Sabella Arquitetura crowns Brazilian house with gridded timber roof

"The conception of a very simple and easily executable construction system reflects a concern for the realities of the local workforce," it contniued.

"The construction technique, the modular arrangement of the structural components, and the ribs of the double-tee floor slabs are all clearly legible."

Rooms feature artful decor and a neutral colour palette. The ground level contains an open-plan kitchen, dining area and living room, along with service areas and a guest bedroom.

The communal area opens toward a garden, and beyond it, a sheltered barbecue terrace and a swimming pool.

"The social areas were conceived as one large veranda in direct contact with the beach sand, with views of both the sea and mountains," the team said.

The upper level contains four bedrooms, including the primary suite, and a family room. A bridge passes over the garden below and connects to a concrete terrace with sweeping views of the sea.

Other projects by Estudio 41 include a small white house in Brazil with a roof garden, and a prefabricated, teal-coloured research station in Antarctica.

## Keep tabs on Parliament.

### What we’re doing

Finding out what your representatives in Ottawa are up to can be tough.We’re trying to make it easy.

Find your MP by entering your postal code above. See what your representatives are saying, and what laws they’re proposing. Poke around.

### What they’re talking about

The latest House transcript is from Thursday, November 26th, when the word of the day was c-31. The House is sitting today; transcripts are usually available the next morning. These are the topics that were discussed.

This summary is computer-generated. Usually it’s accurate, but every now and then it’ll contain inaccuracies or total fabrications.

Exercise of Powers Under the Building Canada Act Members present a committee report on the Building Canada Act, while Conservative and Bloc dissenting opinions raise concerns about transparency, oversight, conflicts of interest, environmental safeguards, Indigenous and workers’ rights, and youth perspectives. 600 words.

Petitions

Pacific wild salmon fundingPesticide regulation and reassessmentBring Shen Yun to OttawaSanctions against Alex OvechkinDeclare U.S. Ambassador persona non grata

Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2 Third reading of Bill C-31. The bill implements measures from the 2025 budget, including tax incentives, changes to labour and benefit rules, pesticide regulation amendments, and a Defence Investment Agency. Liberal members say it supports investment, economic resilience and faster defence procurement; opposition members criticize its timing and omnibus format, and raise concerns about debt, transparency, oversight and the effects of specific provisions. 48400 words, 5 hours in 2 segments: 12.

Ability of Member to Represent Constituents Members debate a question of privilege concerning alleged threats against a veteran and nurse after she spoke with her MP, emphasizing constituents’ right to contact representatives without intimidation and support for a full examination. 400 words.

Question Period

The Conservatives focus on alleged conflicts of interest and insider benefits in government contracts, including Telesat and Cohere, and demand scrutiny of the Prime Minister’s wife’s ocean envoy role. They oppose the Alto rail project, criticize the carbon tax’s impact on auto jobs, and call for tougher responses to home invasions, dangerous driving, and child exploitation. They also raise airport security and Arctic energy concerns. The Liberals defend investments in Telesat and Cohere, support for auto workers and jobs, and the Alto rail project and broader infrastructure agenda, which they say can protect farmland and meet environmental standards. They also highlight tougher crime laws, cadet funding, support for the Rohingya, and investment in national parks. The Bloc criticize the Alto project’s expropriation powers and its impact on affected residents and farmers, while condemning Bill C-39 for bypassing environmental protections and Indigenous consultation. They also accuse the government of echoing Trump’s approach. The NDP press the government to uphold international law amid the Gaza conflict and oppose Parks Canada cuts, warning of risks to visitor safety, conservation, and Indigenous partnerships.

items.body:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled [“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”](https://calnewport.com/the-deep-life-some-notes/) As I explained:

> “To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote [several](https://calnewport.com/on-productivity-and-the-deep-life/) [more](https://calnewport.com/work-and-the-deep-life/) [essays](https://calnewport.com/more-on-cultivating-a-deep-life-mindset/) on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I [launched my podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/at/podcast/ep-1-my-new-task-system-deep-work-with-kids-and/id1515786216?i=1000476077409), I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, [ The Deep Life: A Structured Approach ](https://www.thedeeplife.com/), is now [available for pre-order](https://www.thedeeplife.com/).

*The Deep Life* brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend [Oliver Burkeman](https://www.amazon.com/Four-Thousand-Weeks-Management-Mortals/dp/1250849357/), to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

> “It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is *the* *key* that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

- [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach/dp/0593544870/)
- [Barnes & Noble](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/the-deep-life-cal-newport/1150475131)
- [Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/p/books/the-deep-life-tk-cal-newport/e0548b9282c19397)
- [Amazon UK](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach-Meaning/dp/024184777X?maas=maas_adg_5415FAC779DFD0467C9715278D881B94_afap_abs&ref_=aa_maas&tag=maas&th=1)
- [Waterstones ](https://www.waterstones.com/book/9780241847770?sv1=affiliate&sv_campaign_id=117976&awc=3787_1794332947_70780920f00186c80dbe28e794089d47&utm_source=117976&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=Penguin+Books)

You can also pre-order [ a signed copy ](https://peoplesbooktakoma.com/product/the-deep-life/) from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, **I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it**, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

items.title: Going by; Laughing; Living.
items.subtitle: The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

items.body:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

I wonder if people can listen with their hearts.

I wonder if people can look at trees right in their eyes.

Just like they can go by,

Just like they can laugh,

Just like they can live.

I hope they can look at trees right in their eyes.

And tell them they are sorry.

Stop going by.

Stop laughing.

Stop living if just for a moment.

And tell them they are sorry.

I hope people can be alone and look at themselves.

At the sky full of pink, and orange, and yellow.

Hear all this scary noise they are making. Hear it with their hearts.

Then maybe they can all be silent, we can all be silent.

Be silent while all around it's getting dark.
And wait the night out.

Wait alongside the trees, the rivers, the critters running under our feet.

Tell them all they are precious,

That we never meant it and that we are sorry.

Maybe then I can go by.

Maybe then I can laugh.

Maybe then I can live.

items.body:
## Minimalist Beach House Doubles as a Frame for the Ocean It Overlooks

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/casa-malonic-hw-studio/)

Casa Malonic, or Malonic House, is a recently completed residential project in the beach town of Zihuatanejo, Mexico. But this is no ordinary beach house. Instead, it serves the striking oceanic landscape at its feet. Conceived by Mexico-based firm [HW Studio](https://www.hw-studio.com/), the entire design draws from two defining elements: the land it sits on and its colors, resulting in a construction that engages in a soft yet profound dialogue with the surrounding environment.

This gentle approach is almost a secret, for those who come across Casa Malonic from the street would see only a white mass wrapped in a single curved wall that almost signals [brutalism](https://mymodernmet.com/brutalist-architecture/). As the dwellers step inside, the entrance path leads to a circular courtyard where a soothing transition begins, as if the house sheds concrete layers to reveal its true nature. The walls then give way to a boundless view of the ocean and the surrounding landscape.

When first approaching the construction site, the architects were so fascinated by the area that they wanted to spotlight it. They made a point to honor the elements that predated the architecture: flora, fauna, topography, and sunlight. To do that, they reduced architecture to ground, roof, and shadow—its most basic elements. They found inspiration in an *enramada*, a simple shelter beneath a canopy that, even at its barest, can provide shade and protection from rain without enforcing a strict boundary.

This concept is what creates the most striking feature of Casa Malonic. Rather than providing just another floor-to-ceiling window or glass balcony to take in the beach landscape, the entire structure doubles as a frame for the horizon line. It’s also through this choice that the architects declare this view the spiritual heart of the house. To them, the horizon line is what makes the design possible; not the other way around.

Meant to be taken in as an all-encompassing habitat, the oceanic imagery is not limited to the views. The flooring imitates color and texture, evoking the sand below, as if establishing one continuous path to it. The white walls match the landscape by recalling the flowers of the nine Cacalosúchil trees that surround the house.

“The materiality does not seek to represent the landscape, but to establish a sensory continuity with it. Architecture is first experienced through the feet, before it is understood through the eyes,” writes HW Studio. “The project does not seek to reproduce nature, nor to disappear completely into it. It seeks to construct a precise relationship with the site through a few operations: contain, move through, subtract, and open. The house is ultimately understood as a balance between matter and void.”

To stay up to date with this architecture firm, follow [HW Studio on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/hwstudioarq/).
